title: Agentic AI for grid operators
kicker: Agentic AI for grid operators · three-hour workshop
takeaway: Build an evidence trail before asking an operator to act.
notes: Begin with the operator's task rather than the software package. A recommendation becomes useful when someone can identify its inputs, inspect the calculation, and understand why it passed or failed a declared check. Ask the audience to keep one recurring question in mind: what evidence would change your decision? The workshop connects graph execution, engineering models, learned controllers, language-model responses, and human review. Each component has a different responsibility. We will use an illustrative graph first, then the existing numerical notebooks. The feeder study is a synthetic Greensboro example, not a live utility deployment. Reveal the three learning actions individually. Transition: an operator encounters three kinds of decisions, and the same evidence discipline must survive all three.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Three decisions; one discipline
takeaway: The mathematical task changes; the requirement for traceable evidence remains.
items: Voltage: choose a continuous inverter command
Restoration: choose permitted paths and served loads
Cyber response: decide which measurements support control
prompt: What must an operator see before accepting any of these?
answer: The exact candidate, declared model, checked limits, evidence age, and unresolved assumptions.

refs.label: Tutorial notebooks · three declared case scopes

notes: Invite one short answer before revealing the three cases. Voltage support concerns continuous active and reactive control. Restoration includes discrete decisions and load priorities. Cyber response concerns the reliability of the information used to estimate and control a state. These are not three names for the same optimization problem. The tutorial therefore changes its numerical method while retaining a shared record and explicit verification. Keep the question grounded: an operator needs evidence for this candidate in this case, not a general claim that the language model is capable. Later results will include ties, rejected commands, and a model-scope mismatch. Transition: turn these practical needs into three things participants should be able to do at the end.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: What you will be able to explain
takeaway: Explain the graph, reproduce a decision, and defend an acceptance or hold.
items: Trace state through every proposed stage
Match code, equations, outputs, and timing boundaries
Separate numerical benefit from workflow benefit
prompt: If the final objective ties the baseline, what could still improve?
answer: Inspectability or stale-evidence rejection may improve; those benefits need their own measurements.
notes: State the assessment criteria plainly. A successful participant can point to the node that produced a value, connect a displayed equation to the notebook operation, and explain the final review status. Do not equate the presence of several agents with improved control. The workflow might organize evidence better while producing the same command as a conventional program. Conversely, it might spend more time without improving either result. This is why we separate numerical quality, trace quality, and latency. The labs deliberately include an ordinary-Python baseline and matched engineering comparisons. Use the audience question to make a null numerical result scientifically useful. Transition: show when participants will learn each concept and when they will run it.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: A three-hour route with experiments throughout
takeaway: Each case follows concepts, an executable experiment, and an evidence-based discussion.
rows: L2–L5; archived and optional live Llama
notes: The course is a single teaching sequence; the technical explanations and exercises are part of the lecture. Software installation is a prerequisite, not an activity to begin during the first exercise. Ask participants to open both notebooks now while keeping their current kernels separate. The graph notebook teaches orchestration with transparent arithmetic. The classroom notebook performs the engineering experiments and reads explicitly labeled archived language-model responses. A fresh calculation, a saved actual response, and a newly generated model response are different evidence modes. Preserve those labels when discussing speed or quality. The schedule reserves time for prediction and explanation rather than continuous lecturing. Transition: before opening the first code cell, identify what makes a workflow agentic.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: A useful agent closes a feedback loop
kicker: From answering to acting through tools
takeaway: A returned tool result can change the next permitted operation.
notes: Reveal the loop one action at a time. ReAct is an influential example of combining language-model deliberation with external actions and observations. Our teaching emphasis is the observable interface: what operation was requested, what result came back, and how the next decision used it. We do not need access to private model reasoning to inspect those steps. A predefined workflow follows known routes; an agent can choose among permitted operations using the current context. Real applications can mix both patterns. In this tutorial, deterministic routing and numerical limits constrain language-selected trials. A loop does not by itself establish reliability or intelligence. Transition: separate the component choosing an operation from the component calculating its result and the runtime coordinating both.

title: Tool feedback changes the next choice
kicker: Teaching adaptation of the ReAct interaction pattern
items: A choice requests a bounded tool.
New evidence can change the next choice.
takeaway: The useful loop is a decision updated by an observation.

refs.label: Conceptual adaptation: Yao et al., ReAct (ICLR 2023), CC BY 4.0

notes: This original teaching diagram adapts the interaction pattern explained by ReAct. It replaces the published question-answering example with four neutral operations. Start at the current observation, identify an allowed tool action, execute that action, and read the returned evidence before choosing again. The arrows show information flow. They do not guarantee that the next choice is correct. In the grid tutorial, a numerical verifier may reject the proposed action even when the language explanation sounds plausible. The animation highlights one operation at a time on the same slide. A deterministic retry budget and explicit exit conditions are introduced later, because an unbounded feedback loop can waste computation. Transition: separate the agent making a choice from the tool doing the calculation and the orchestrator enforcing the route.

title: Tool, agent, orchestrator: three different jobs
takeaway: Roles describe responsibilities; they do not require different language-model backbones.
items: Agent: chooses an allowed next operation
Tool: returns a specific calculation or record
Orchestrator: runs routes and stores state
notes: Use a concrete voltage example. A planning role proposes a candidate, a power-flow tool evaluates it, and the runtime requires a verification step before the candidate is eligible for review. The same Llama model can support several role-specific prompts. Numerical functions can perform a role without calling any language model. This distinction prevents a common confusion: five boxes are not necessarily five independent models, five independent opinions, or five levels of protection. The responsibilities are useful because their input and output contracts can be inspected separately. The engineering tutorial implements its orchestration in custom Python; the graph lab introduces LangGraph mechanics separately. Transition: a tool becomes dependable only when its request and response are sufficiently explicit to check.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: A tool call is a small engineering contract
takeaway: A result needs a candidate, units, model scope, and status.
items: Input: case, revision, command, and limits
Output: values, units, convergence, and evidence identity
Failure: explicit error or rejected result
prompt: Does “solver converged” mean the current limit passed?
answer: No. Convergence and operating feasibility are separate checks.
notes: Treat the tool contract like a laboratory measurement sheet. The number 112 is unusable until its unit, location, candidate, and calculation conditions are known. A solver may converge to a state that violates an operating limit. A request may be well formed yet refer to an outdated network. The contract makes these distinctions available to later nodes; it does not resolve them automatically. The tutorial records the candidate and declared context so that verification can inspect a particular calculation. Ask participants to identify which fields a current-limit check needs. Reveal the answer only after someone distinguishes convergence from feasibility. Transition: standardized tool communication can make these contracts reusable across software, but the engineering checks still belong to the application.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Where MCP fits in the picture
takeaway: A common tool interface helps integration; it does not certify the returned engineering result.
notes: Explain Model Context Protocol as an interface layer that exposes tools to an application. A consistent call format can reduce integration work when different engineering packages are involved. The diagram is architectural context, not a claim that our local classroom notebook uses an MCP server. Its functions are called directly in Python. This is a useful distinction between understanding an ecosystem and reproducing a specific implementation. Ask which part would still need to know whether 112 amperes exceeds the permitted rating. That comparison remains application logic using an agreed unit and limit. A transport protocol cannot supply a missing model assumption. Transition: now place the proposal's five responsibilities above the particular tool and transport choices.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: The complete proposed workflow has five stages
takeaway: Every changed candidate must return to simulation and verification.
items: Verification checks; optimization chooses the next trial
notes: Use the animation to carry one candidate through all five proposed stages. Awareness establishes the case and interprets the request. Planning chooses a numerical formulation and produces a candidate. Simulation calculates modeled consequences. Verification checks the declared constraints and evidence consistency. The LLM optimizer proposes or selects permitted follow-up work, which must be evaluated again if it changes the action. Human review is the handoff after these responsibilities, not a replacement for a missing stage. All five are represented in the archived engineering trace later in the course. Some work is deterministic, some uses numerical optimization, and some uses model responses. Transition: identify which responsibility the language model can help with, and which remains a numerical calculation.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Give each stage the method it needs
takeaway: The language model coordinates bounded choices; numerical methods produce and check the physical evidence.
items: Planning: MPC, restoration MILP, or estimation/control
Simulation: LinDistFlow, OpenDSS, or declared teaching model
Verification: explicit numerical and consistency checks
Selection: fixed rule, vote, or learned bandit
notes: Avoid presenting the same algorithm as the natural solution to every case. Continuous voltage support suits the MPC and SAC comparison. Restoration uses a mixed-integer service-allocation formulation. The cyber teaching example combines estimation, anomaly evidence, and a constrained response. These methods are part of the workflow rather than competitors excluded by its design. The language model sees a bounded catalog of permitted operations and returns a choice with a public explanation. The explanation is checked against the numerical evidence; it is not treated as a proof. Learned response selection is a separate, discrete decision from SAC's continuous physical control. Transition: before reading the code, establish a visual vocabulary that clearly separates computation from the electrical network.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Learn four symbols before reading the graph
takeaway: Workflow arrows represent dependencies, not electrical connections.
items: Arrow A → B: B needs A's result
Diamond r(s): choose the permitted next route

symbols.meaning: B requires the result from A
A routing rule evaluated on state

notes: Point to each visual symbol as it appears. A node is a unit of work. State is the record that subsequent work reads. A directed edge identifies an allowed execution dependency. A routing rule chooses a successor based on the current record. Use the same symbol meanings when the diagram becomes code later. The letters here are computational names; they do not identify buses, currents, or physical switches. This matters because later restoration figures also contain nodes and edges, but those edges represent network connections. Ask the audience what an arrow from simulation to verification requires: the verification operation must have a result to inspect. Transition: begin with the simplest dependency structure, one with no path returning to its starting node.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: DAG means directed and acyclic
takeaway: A DAG encodes dependencies without a backward path.
items: B and C inspect independent results
D combines both pieces of evidence
notes: Build the diamond-shaped dependency diagram in place. The example freezes a candidate before checking its voltage and current evidence. The final operation needs both check results. Directed means arrows have an orientation; acyclic means no sequence of arrows returns to its starting operation. Define the node set and edge set without requiring graph theory background. The two middle checks are conceptual operations on already produced evidence. This picture does not claim that two OpenDSS engines run concurrently, and it does not describe the cyclic graph used in the G lab. Let the audience trace each prerequisite with a finger. Transition: more than one valid execution order can preserve the same arrows, which gives us a short prediction exercise.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Which schedule respects every arrow?
takeaway: The join must follow both prerequisites, whatever their order.
answer: The first two. The third starts D before C has supplied its result.
notes: Pause before revealing the validity marks. Ask participants to justify an answer by naming an edge, not by guessing the intended order. Both B and C depend on A, and D depends on both B and C. Therefore the middle operations may exchange positions, while the final operation cannot move ahead of either prerequisite. This is the meaning of a topological order. It describes a valid ordering, not a measured time or speedup. A real scheduler also has resource limits, tool state, and failure handling. If a participant proposes concurrent middle operations, acknowledge that dependencies permit it only when the implementation and resources permit it too. Transition: inspect what must be preserved when work actually branches and later rejoins.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Fan-out and join need a shared identity
kicker: Parallel work is still one experiment
takeaway: Both branches must refer to the same frozen candidate and context.
items: Each branch returns its own evidence
notes: Animate the same candidate identifier into both branches. Then change the identifier on one returned record conceptually and ask whether the results may still be combined. They may not establish a verdict for one common candidate. This is a simple way to teach stale or mismatched evidence without introducing complex concurrency machinery. Parallel execution can reduce elapsed time when work and resources are independent, but it can also create synchronization and merge problems. The tutorial's engineering runs should not be described as parallel simply because this diagram branches. Their timing boundary is measured separately. The visual teaches a design obligation: completeness and identity at the join. Transition: a failed verification adds another kind of edge, one that deliberately goes back for a revised calculation.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: A repair loop is a cycle, with a budget
takeaway: A finite retry budget bounds attempts; it does not guarantee a feasible command.
items: Fail with budget → repair and simulate again
notes: Trace the success path first, then reveal the backward repair edge. Once that edge exists, the program graph is cyclic and should not be called a DAG. A finite individual execution can still be drawn as a sequence of visits. The two integer symbols count used and allowed repairs. The tutorial increments the counter when it modifies the command and sends that command back through simulation. A finite count guarantees that this policy eventually stops if its tool calls return; separate timeouts would be needed for a stalled tool. Holding is a valid outcome when no admissible command is found within the budget. Transition: the router needs both the latest verdict and the counter, so these values must live in shared state.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: State is the laboratory record carried forward
takeaway: A node reads state and returns explicit updates to the record.
items: Control flow: attempts, budget, and status
Trace: the sequence of recorded events

symbols.meaning: Returned field updates; not arithmetic subtraction

notes: Read the displayed record as a laboratory notebook with named fields. The command identifies what was proposed, the evidence fields identify what was calculated, and the control-flow fields identify what should happen next. The merge expression is a conceptual description of applying returned updates. Delta is not a numerical difference between two entire records. The G notebook uses TypedDict to describe expected keys and types, while its initial-state function explicitly validates numerical inputs. TypedDict itself does not perform runtime value checking. A chat transcript alone is not a substitute for this engineering record because important values and units must be easy to locate and compare. Transition: different fields need different rules when new information arrives.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Replace a result; append an event
takeaway: The merge rule is part of the data model.
items: Parallel writes need an explicit compatible rule
prompt: Should a repaired command keep the previous current as its current result?
answer: No. Replace the current result; preserve the previous event in the trace.

symbols.meaning: Reducer combining stored value and update
Existing event list and new event list

notes: Use the animation to replace the scalar value while visibly extending the event list. The current field describes the latest simulated command, so retaining the old value there would be misleading. The trace field describes history, so discarding earlier events would make the repair difficult to inspect. The example's plus symbol means list concatenation, not arithmetic averaging or consensus. In the code, Annotated attaches the addition function to the trace field. An empty appended list does not erase existing events. If several branches write a field, the application needs a merge rule appropriate to that field and its ordering semantics. Transition: after updating the record, one small routing function can choose among success, repair, and hold.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Routing turns evidence into the next step
takeaway: Verification computes the verdict; routing chooses what to do with it.
items: passed = false and k < K → repair
passed = false and k ≥ K → hold
notes: Reveal the mutually exclusive conditions in order. The first condition checks whether the latest calculation passed. If it did not, the second decision is whether a repair is still permitted. The route returns a label, and the graph maps that label to a node. This policy is deliberately deterministic so that participants can reason about every execution path. A more flexible language-selected operation could be inserted elsewhere without allowing it to bypass these acceptance conditions. Ask what would happen if the counter were equal to the budget: the route must hold. The numerical verification rule and the orchestration policy remain separate functions. Transition: a report can itself pause for review, which requires saved execution state.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Checkpoint: remember where the workflow stopped
takeaway: A checkpoint associates execution state with a thread identifier.
notes: Use a bookmark analogy, then make it precise with the stored record and pending node. In the G lab, a thread identifier associates the checkpoint with a particular execution. That identifier is not an operator credential. The example uses InMemorySaver, so the state remains available in the running process but does not provide durable recovery after the kernel disappears. This scope is sufficient for observing a pause and resume during class. Participants should inspect the snapshot before discussing its final status; otherwise a whole-cell execution can make the pause easy to miss. The upcoming exercise prints the pending node and acknowledgment flag. Transition: an interrupt exposes the question that a human or caller must answer before that execution can continue.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Interrupt: make the review decision visible
takeaway: A review response must identify the recommendation it acknowledges.
items: Pause with candidate and evidence scope
Resume with an explicit matching response
notes: Distinguish a visible recommendation from an acknowledged recommendation. The toy sends an interrupt payload that includes a recommendation identifier, command, calculated value, and declared scope. Its scripted reply must approve the same identifier. A wrong identifier or a declined response remains distinguishable from approval. This demonstrates a record-consistency mechanism, not operator authentication or equipment dispatch. On resumption, the interrupted node can begin again, so uncontrolled side effects before the interrupt would be a design problem. The toy only records state changes. Ask participants what the operator should see if the candidate changes while review is pending. The answer motivates fresh evidence and a new identity. Transition: organize these requirements into three checks that answer different questions.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Typed, current, feasible: three separate claims
takeaway: Passing one check does not establish the others.
items: Binding: is this result for this candidate?
prompt: The solve converged at 112 A; the limit is 100 A. Verdict?
answer: Reject that candidate under the declared current limit.
notes: Keep this slide concrete rather than reading a compliance checklist. Give the current example verbally and ask for the verdict before revealing it. A converged solver result can fail a physical operating condition. A correctly shaped result can be stale. A matching hash can identify consistent data without proving who produced it. These checks are complementary because they answer different questions. Our later lab uses an explicitly illustrative payload to isolate the binding mechanism; participants must not mistake its passed field for a real feeder calculation. The final operator packet adds another distinction between evidence scope and the requested scope. Transition: ask what happens when a favorable language-model explanation conflicts with a failed numerical check.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: A vote cannot raise a declared limit
takeaway: Selection chooses a trial; verification determines whether it is admissible.
prompt: Can a majority vote make this candidate acceptable?
answer: No. Reject it, preserve the incumbent, and record the failed margin.
notes: Use the fictional numbers as a fast diagnostic question. The source of a candidate and the number of models supporting it do not change its calculated current or the stated limit. The selected operation has earned a trial, not automatic acceptance. A failed trial should leave the previous admissible candidate available and should produce an inspectable rejection record. The later voltage experiment implements this separation between response selection and numerical evaluation. Multiple models may also share errors, so agreement does not establish independent evidence. This lesson is compatible with both conventional supervisors and agentic workflows. Transition: close the concept sequence by showing which existing research frameworks contribute related mechanisms, using qualified claims rather than a promotional ranking.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: PowerAgent: connect engineering capabilities
takeaway: Reusable tool interfaces and workflows reduce integration effort across applications.
items: Capabilities vary with the selected application
notes: Present PowerAgent as a roadmap and ecosystem rather than one immutable controller. Its official materials organize domain capabilities through tools and reusable workflows. The teaching connection is our tool-contract slide: a clearly defined interface can make the same numerical capability usable from different applications. The diagram on this slide is a tutorial schematic of that concept, not a reproduced architecture figure. Do not infer an ecosystem-wide acceptance guarantee from the availability of a tool. In class, ask which fields an OpenDSS wrapper should return so that a different planner can still use its result. This turns a literature example into a design exercise. Transition: a connected collection of tools still needs protection against using them in an invalid order.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: PowerDAG: check prerequisite relationships
takeaway: A one-shot advisory detects a covered prerequisite violation; repeated calls may proceed.
items: Check prerequisite tool writes within covered scope
One-shot advisory; repeated calls may proceed
notes: PowerDAG combines exemplar retrieval with deterministic checks of selected tool prerequisites. Its inspected study reports 30 unseen queries, 50 expert exemplars, and 82 tools. Section IV-C2 describes a one-shot advisory: an initial covered violation is blocked, but repeating the call is permitted. This is not an unconditional hard safety gate. Relate the mechanism to our fan-out identity example while retaining that distinction. The cited figure exposes the paper architecture; our classroom code illustrates a narrower evidence-binding idea. Ask what our own application should require after the load changes: evidence associated with the new context. Our guard rejects stale binding explicitly. Transition: the next framework emphasizes what happens after a proposed physical change fails in a sandbox.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.
image_caption: Badmus & Pandey (2026), Fig. 2, CC BY-SA 4.0. Unchanged figure.

title: Grid-Agent: test a change before retaining it
takeaway: A failed trial should not silently replace the incumbent.
items: Evaluate actions in a simulation sandbox
Retain or roll back using returned evidence

refs.label: Zhang et al. · Grid-Agent · v3, 2025 preprint

notes: The inspected Grid-Agent version describes five roles and a sandbox workflow with validation and rollback. Its role names are Topology, Planner, Executor, Validator, and Summarizer. This is close prior art for splitting grid work among specialized responsibilities, so our teaching workflow should not claim to invent five-agent grid verification. The useful classroom question is whether a rejected candidate can accidentally become the retained command. Use the paper figure to locate the validation loop, then connect it to our separate incumbent and trial records. The v3 source recommends human oversight for deployment; it does not establish that every demonstrated action underwent authenticated operator approval. Transition: another architecture separates planning from coordination and domain-tool execution, which helps explain why state handoffs matter.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.
image_caption: Zhang et al. (2025), Grid-Agent v3, Fig. 1, CC BY 4.0. Unchanged.

title: X-GridAgent: separate planning, coordination, and action
takeaway: A hierarchy helps organize work only when each handoff preserves the required context.
items: Action selects domain tools and reads results
notes: X-GridAgent organizes power-grid analysis in three layers and exposes domain capabilities through multiple tool servers. Its study uses 11 representative queries repeated 30 times, not 330 distinct tasks. The source also describes retrieval and prompt refinement. For our teaching purpose, focus on one mechanism: a plan needs coordination, and coordination needs an action interface that returns usable evidence. Ask which information must survive all three layers. The candidate, model scope, limits, and task identity are stronger answers than an unstructured summary alone. This slide is an independently drawn teaching schematic of the conceptual hierarchy; it is not an altered paper figure. Transition: compare these mechanisms compactly while preserving the qualifications hidden by a simple checkmark.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Read the ticks as scope, not a league table
takeaway: Cross-paper capability marks do not establish a common performance ranking.
items: Different tasks, models, budgets, and evaluation boundaries
Benchmark work evaluates agents; it is not a controller
Our benefit must be tested against matched baselines
notes: Define the marks before interpreting the rows. A tick records a documented capability in the inspected source; a triangle preserves a qualification; NR means not reported in that source rather than proved absent. PowerAgent capabilities vary by workflow. PowerDAG covers selected dependencies with a one-shot advisory. Grid-Agent oversight is proposed for deployment. X-GridAgent includes solver checks and human prompt refinement. PowerAgentBench-SS supplies an evaluation protocol with hidden revalidation under a DC scope. The tutorial's review tick refers to local advisory readback, not authenticated field authorization. None of these rows forms a shared performance benchmark. Ask what would make a valid benefit claim: common scenarios, tools, budgets, outcome definitions, and timing boundaries. Transition: run a transparent graph and its ordinary-Python baseline before introducing electrical complexity.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: Our first experiment makes every transition visible
takeaway: Learn real graph execution with deliberately simple arithmetic.
notes: Announce the switch from concepts to the first executable exercise. The response law is invented for teaching; it is not a feeder model, a power-flow approximation, an MPC controller, or a learned policy. Its simplicity lets participants predict each value and inspect every route. LangGraph execution is real, including the conditional edge, checkpoint, interrupt, and resume. The repair subtracts 0.25 from the command without allowing it below zero. The verification compares the resulting illustrative current with the declared limit. We will compare graph execution with a direct-Python loop using identical functions, so the experiment isolates orchestration. Transition: open the notebook and first establish which runtime is actually being used.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: G0: confirm the runtime and the experiment boundary
takeaway: Record the installed versions before interpreting the execution.
items: Disables external tracing in this lab
Prints versions and the toy scope
notes: Run the complete G0 cell, even though the slide displays only its relevant lines. Confirm that the version dictionary appears before proceeding. The captured run used LangGraph 1.2.15, checkpoint 4.3.0, and langchain-core 1.6.12; a participant's environment may differ. The cell disables the external tracing flags used by this exercise and declares that no language-model or electrical-model validation occurs. After dependencies are installed, the toy needs no Ollama service. If imports fail, use the supplied graph-lab requirements and return to the documented setup rather than changing the experiment during class. This practical boundary keeps the graph lesson reproducible. Transition: define the record that every subsequent node will read and update.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: G1: turn the record into a state schema
takeaway: The schema names fields; the trace annotation selects its merge rule.
items: command and limit describe the trial
prompt: After simulate and verify append one event each, how many remain?
answer: Two events; the list-addition reducer keeps both.
notes: Highlight the control fields first, then the verdict fields, then the trace annotation. Run the complete G1 cell so the audience also sees the initial validated state and the list-addition example below this excerpt. TypedDict states the intended record structure; initial_state performs the example's explicit input validation. These two mechanisms should not be confused. The trace is a sequence of recorded events, not an internal chain of thought and not a cryptographically authenticated audit log. Ask participants to predict the number of trace entries before revealing the answer. This is the same replace-versus-append idea they saw conceptually. Transition: the first node uses the command to calculate a value, and the next node compares it with the limit.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: G2: a node returns only its updates
takeaway: The calculation and the acceptance test are inspectable functions.
prompt: For u = 0.75 and L = 0.80, does verification pass?
answer: i = 1.00, so the first verification fails.

refs.label: G2 · exact simulate and verify functions

notes: Read the first function as an ordinary Python calculation. It returns current and a trace update rather than reconstructing the entire state record. The next function compares that current with the limit using a small numerical tolerance. The tolerance addresses floating-point comparison in this toy; it is not an engineering margin. With command 0.75, the result is 1.00 and the limit is 0.80, so the verdict is false. That outcome is expected rather than a program error. Ask which returned field the router will inspect. Run the entire G2 cell, including the repair and terminal-node definitions that follow this excerpt. Transition: inspect the four lines that convert the verdict and budget into a route.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: G2: the route is four readable lines
takeaway: A successful test reports; a failed test repairs only while budget remains.
notes: Map each code branch to the earlier route diagram. The successful branch returns report. The failed branch compares the completed repair count with the maximum and returns either repair or hold. Because the same functions will be supplied to the direct-Python baseline, any numerical difference would indicate an implementation issue rather than a more intelligent graph. Ask what happens after one repair when the maximum is one and the verification still fails. The answer is hold, since equality means the budget is exhausted. A recursion limit also appears at invocation, but that runtime limit is not the application repair policy. Transition: node functions and route labels still need connections before they form an executable graph.
animation: Reveal the question or diagram first, then the method or result, then the takeaway; retain one slide.

title: G3: wire the functions into the diagram
takeaway: Edges permit execution paths; compilation does not prove the engineering assumptions.
items: Verification selects report, repair, or hold
notes: Run G3 and confirm the compiled node list. Highlight the fixed edge from simulate to verify, the conditional edge that calls route, and the edge returning repair to simulate. The mapping translates a returned label into a permitted successor. The report and hold nodes terminate this version of the execution. Compilation checks structural requirements of the graph; it is not a proof that the chosen response law describes a feeder or that the repair rule finds an optimum. notes: Define the two broad approaches before naming the particular algorithms. Model-based control uses predicted behavior in an optimization problem; the displayed expression omits constraints for clarity, and the voltage lesson supplies them explicitly. Model-free learning trains an action rule through experience and rewards. It may obtain that experience from a simulator, so model-free does not mean no simulator was used. MPC plans over a horizon and applies its first action. SAC supplies continuous control from saved learned weights in class. PPO is a relevant continuous-action alternative but is not trained in this tutorial. Training cost and inference cost are separate. Both proposed commands must be simulated and checked under the same declared limits. Transition: leave the illustrative graph and establish a fair experiment on the selected feeder models.
